bull_case: AI increases content volume and Adobe monetizes the resulting workflow complexity across creation, documents and marketing.
bear_case: Model-native competitors can weaken application lock-in and pricing power faster than Adobe's AI products offset it.
thesis: Adobe still occupies category-defining positions in creative tooling, documents and enterprise digital experience. AI expands content volume and productivity demand, but also lowers switching costs at the generation layer; Adobe's durability depends on owning end-to-end workflows, not only creation models.

evidence.claim: Q2 Creative & Marketing Professionals subscription revenue grew 13%.
Q2 Business Professionals & Consumers subscription revenue grew 16%.

counterevidence: AI lowers content-creation barriers and could shift value from application vendors toward models, distribution layers or new agentic workflows.
unknowns: Long-run AI monetization per user, Firefly inference economics, and how much AI-first ARR is incremental versus bundled/reclassified ARR.
falsifiers: If ARR growth falls to low single digits while AI usage rises, or owner FCF/share stops compounding despite buybacks, the moat/compounder thesis is downgraded.
next_checks: Q4/FY2026 ARR, AI-first ARR, OCF, SBC, repurchases, share count and Digital Media/Experience growth

subscores.rationale: Digital content, document productivity and customer experience remain long-duration software demand pools.
Photoshop, Acrobat, Creative Cloud and Experience Cloud remain category-defining workflow standards.
AI creates real substitution risk, but Adobe has multiple independent product/customer growth axes.

uncertainties.rationale: AI monetization and competitive workflow migration remain the central uncertainty.
